title: Flavonoid Profiling by Liquid Chromatography Coupled to Mass Spectrometry
author: Camilo E. Vital
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.zggf3tw
materials: Fragment relative intensity (FRI%) from Kaempferol and Luteolin:

steps.title: Collect and freeze plant tissue
steps.instruction: Collect plant tissue samples, immediately freeze in liquid nitrogen and store at –80 °C until use.

steps.title: Macerate and weigh tissue
steps.instruction: Keep samples frozen, macerate in liquid nitrogen with a mortar and pestle (do not allow to thaw), weigh approximately 100 mg of each sample into 2 mL microtubes and record the exact weight.

steps.title: Add extraction solvent
steps.instruction: Add 200 µL of a solution containing 75 % methanol and 0.1 % formic acid to each tube.

steps.title: Sonicate and centrifuge (first extract)
steps.instruction: Sonicate the tubes for 30 minutes, then centrifuge at 14 000 g for 10 minutes at 4 °C and transfer the supernatant to a new tube.

steps.title: Repeat extraction on pellet
steps.instruction: Add a second 200 µL aliquot of the 75 % methanol/0.1 % formic acid solution to the remaining pellet, sonicate 30 minutes, centrifuge 14 000 g for 10 minutes at 4 °C, collect the supernatant and pool it with the first supernatant.

steps.title: Filter pooled extract
steps.instruction: Filter the pooled supernatant through a disposable 0.2 mL PVDF membrane.

steps.title: Dry and reconstitute extract
steps.instruction: Dry the filtrate in a speed‑vacuum concentrator and re‑dissolve the residue in 50 µL deionized water.

steps.title: Store extracts before analysis
steps.instruction: Store the reconstituted extracts at –80 °C until LC‑MS analysis.

steps.title: Configure UHPLC‑MS system
steps.instruction: Set up the UHPLC with 50 µL sample vials and a 5 µL injection loop; install an analytical Zorbax Eclipse Plus C18 column (1.8 µm, 2.1 × 50 mm) with a Zorbax SB‑C18 guard column (1.8 µm). Prepare mobile phase A (water + 0.02 % acetic acid) and B (acetonitrile + 0.02 % acetic acid) and apply the gradient below. Set flow to 0.3 mL min⁻¹, column temperature to 30 °C. Operate a triple‑quadrupole MS in positive ESI mode with gas temperature 300 °C, nitrogen flow 10 L min⁻¹, nebulizer pressure 35 psi, capillary voltage 4000 V, and enable product, precursor and MRM scans.

steps.title: Prepare flavonoid stock standards
steps.instruction: Dissolve each target flavonoid to a concentration of 1.0 µg mL⁻¹ in 50 % methanol and aliquot the solutions into vials.

steps.title: Optimize product ion scans
steps.instruction: For each standard, run a product‑ion scan and adjust transmission and fragmentation parameters (manually or automatically) to obtain the most intense fragment ions; select these ions to build the MRM transition list (Table 1).

steps.title: Create serial dilutions
steps.instruction: Prepare serial dilutions of each standard ranging from 0.1 ng mL⁻¹ to 1.0 ng mL⁻¹ (two replicates per level) according to the mass‑spectrometer sensitivity and linearity.

steps.title: Inject standards and acquire MRM
steps.instruction: Inject 5.0 µL of each dilution using the MRM method defined in the previous step and acquire the data.

steps.title: Generate calibration curves in Skyline
steps.instruction: Import the raw standard data into Skyline, extract ion chromatograms (XICs) for each transition, export the XIC areas to Excel, and plot XIC area versus concentration to obtain linear calibration curves (ng mL⁻¹) for each compound.

steps.title: Inject plant extracts (MRM)
steps.instruction: Randomly inject each plant extract (5 µL) using the same MRM method and acquire raw data.

steps.title: Quantify flavonoids in samples
steps.instruction: Export sample XIC areas from Skyline to Excel, calculate the concentration (ng mL⁻¹) using the corresponding calibration curve, then convert to ng g⁻¹ fresh tissue by multiplying by the factor 1000 µL / 50 µL = 20 (e.g., 420.4 ng mL⁻¹ → 8408 ng g⁻¹; the example in the text shows 420.4 ng mL⁻¹ corresponding to 210 ng g⁻¹ for a 100 mg sample).

steps.title: Optimize glycoconjugate MRM method
steps.instruction: Inject glycoconjugate standards (e.g., rutin, hesperidin, naringin) to adjust in‑source energy for optimal aglycone release before the first quadrupole; inject aglycone standards (daidzein, apigenin, genistein, etc.) to optimize product‑ion scans, avoiding high source energy and using optimal transmission; verify class‑specific fragment ions; build an MRM method with four transitions per compound (Table 2).

steps.title: Acquire glycoconjugate MRM data and FRI%
steps.instruction: Inject the glycoconjugate standards using the MRM method from the previous step, import the data into Skyline, export XIC areas and calculate fragment‑relative‑intensity percentages (FRI %) for each transition; export the FRI % values to Excel to serve as signatures for each compound.

steps.title: Analyze samples for glycoconjugates (in‑source/MRM)
steps.instruction: Randomly inject all plant extracts using the in‑source/MRM setup (section 3.4); process the raw spectra in Skyline to obtain XIC areas and FRI % for each retention time; assign a compound to a given aglycone when its FRI % matches that of a standard.

steps.title: Perform precursor ion scans
steps.instruction: Re‑inject all samples, set up a precursor‑ion scan for each flavonoid class using the parameters of section 3.5, process the data with the instrument’s software (e.g., MassHunter), annotate precursor m/z values for each retention time, subtract 1.0 Da (deprotonated ion) and search each m/z in MassBank (tolerance 0.3 Da) and the literature; subtract the aglycone mass from the precursor m/z to infer the attached sugar moiety.

steps.title: Skyline data analysis workflow
steps.instruction: Install Skyline (32‑ or 64‑bit). Generate a transition‑list table according to the MRM parameters (Table 1). Open the list in OpenOffice, copy all rows except the header. In Skyline create a new document, choose Insert → Transition List, edit the column headings to match the file, paste the data and check for errors, then click Insert. Open Settings → Transitions Settings and configure for QqQ data, then save the settings. Import raw .d files via File → Import → Results, click OK and save the project. View Retention Times → Replicate Comparison and Peak Areas → Replicate Comparison; double‑click the tabs to open the tables. Edit each chromatogram baseline by dragging the dashed line to correct peak integration as needed for every compound and sample. Save the project. Export a report via File → Export → Report, select “Transition Results”, click OK to obtain a spreadsheet of peak areas. Open the spreadsheet in OpenOffice and use the XIC areas for quantitative calculations.
